notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0057.tlg038.1st1K-gr: Title: ΕΤΧΥΜΙΑΣ is a scanning error for ΕΥΧΥΜΙΑΣ ('good humours'). 'Another of my [friends]': τῶν ἐμαυτοῦ is elliptical; 'friends' or 'companions' is implied.

Printed ὠπτήθησυν read as ὠπτήθησαν; τρυ γόνων as τρυγόνων. The text names 'Philotimus' (Φιλότιμον); my rendering 'Phylotimus' should read Philotimus. *oniskoi* (ὀνίσκοι), a fish not securely identified (perhaps a kind of cod or hake). *rhyemata* and *kribanitai* left untranslated: exact kinds of pastry/bread uncertain. κρέας χοίρειον rendered 'pork'.

Both lines share one reference. *Bōlitai* (βωλῖται) are probably Caesar's mushroom (Amanita caesarea) rather than modern boletes. The last sentence of line 2 ('Let us go back... adding') is awkward in the Greek and may be corrupt. The *patētos* date is literally 'trodden'; the exact variety is uncertain. ἄμυλον is taken as starch (wheat starch preparation). The Herodotus named with Euryphon is the physician, not the historian.

Line 5.1: 'as others do with stomachs' (τὰς κοιλίας) is odd in context; the text may be corrupt. *ōchroi* and *dolichoi* are pulses not securely identified (perhaps a vetch and a cowpea). Line 6.1: the sentence on the muscles of eyes ('in those animals whose nature is suited to good humour, such as pigs') is awkwardly constructed and may be corrupt or lacunose; it seems to pass from eye-muscles to the flesh of pigs. 'Stray ἡ.' in 5.1 ('ἡ. διαφορὰ') read as ἡ διαφορά.

Several pulses, cereals and wild plants are left in italics as their identification is uncertain: *ōchroi*, *dolichoi*, *olyra*, *tiphē*, *elymos*/*melinē*, *chondrilē*, *skandix*, *gingidion*, *seris*. 'Persian [fruits]' are presumably peaches. *Sykamina* may be mulberries or sycamore figs; it is distinguished here from *mora*. *Oniskoi* (a soft-fleshed fish, perhaps a kind of hake) and *karkinas* (food of red mullets, perhaps a small crab or a seaweed) are unidentified. In 8.1 'βραδύνουσαι δύνουσαι' is a dittography, read as βραδύνουσαι; 'νῶν' read as νῦν.

Βικυὸς: name of this wine not identified; possibly corrupt. Θηρίνου after Καρυΐνου may be a corruption (perhaps for a variant of Θηραίου); rendered 'Therine'. Κέκουβον taken as Latin caecubum (Caecuban), though Galen here uses it for any much-aged wine. The clause 'μὴ ψυχρῶν δὲ, ὅσοις τούτων οὐδέτερον ὑπάρχει' is obscure, perhaps lacunose; translated literally. 'Τμωλίτης' read for the misspelled 'Τιμωλίτης'.

1: the honey sentence takes ἀλλὰ τῷ γε θερμὸν εἶναι … πᾶν as 'all honey being hot'. ἀποθεραπευτικόν, μέλκη and ἀργιτρόφημα are kept transliterated. In 3, λέπραι are scaly skin diseases, not necessarily leprosy.

nodes.text: GALEN, ON GOOD AND BAD HUMOURS IN FOODS.

The famines that have occurred continually, for not a few years in succession, among many of the peoples subject to the Romans have clearly shown, to those at least who are not wholly senseless, how great a power bad humour has for the generation of diseases. For the city-dwellers, as was their custom to lay in at once during the summer enough grain for the whole following year, took all the wheat from the fields, together with the barley, the beans and the lentils, and left to the country people the other fruits of Demeter, which they call pulses and legumes, while also carrying not a few even of these into the town. So the people in the countryside, having used up what was left during the winter, were forced to use foods producing bad humour throughout the whole spring, eating shoots and sprouts of trees and shrubs, and bulbs, and roots of plants with bad humours, and stuffing themselves too with the so-called wild greens, whatever anyone happened to have plenty of, unsparingly, to the point of surfeit, just as they also boiled and ate whole green herbs which they had never before tasted even by way of trial. One could therefore see some of them at the end of spring, and almost all at the beginning of summer, seized by very many sores forming on the skin, which did not have the same form in all; for some of them were erysipelatous, some inflammatory, some spreading, some lichen-like, and itch-like, and leprous. Of these, the mildest, breaking out through the skin, evacuated the bad humour from the viscera and the depths; but in some people, becoming carbuncular and phagedenic [i.e. eating away the flesh], accompanied by fevers, they killed many over a long time, with scarcely a very few saved. And apart from the affections of the skin there were very many fevers, bringing on foul-smelling and biting evacuations of the bowel, ending in tenesmus and dysenteries, and acrid urine, itself also foul-smelling, which ulcerated the bladder of some. Some of them reached a crisis through sweats, these too foul-smelling, or through putrid abscesses. Those in whom none of these occurred all died, either with evident inflammation of at least one of the viscera, or because of the severity and malignancy of the fevers. When some physicians dared to open a vein in a very few patients at the beginning of the disease (for they were reasonably afraid to use this remedy, because the strength had already been broken down beforehand), I saw in no one good blood drawn off, such as is seen being evacuated from healthy bodies, but either redder, or blacker, or more serous, or acrid and biting the very vein that had been cut as it flowed out, so that the wound became hard to heal. In some, and especially in those who died, there also occurred with the fevers symptoms bringing on damage to the mind, with sleeplessness and lethargic stupor. It is nothing surprising that those who fell ill at that time were seized by opposite diseases and symptoms, since they differed from one another not only in their natures or their ages, but also in their previous regimens, and had eaten during the famine foods having opposite powers. For all ate whatever they had plenty of; but since the supply was unequal, some took foods having sour, or acrid, or salty, or bitter juices, others astringent, or harsh, or clearly cooling, or very moist, or sticky, or drug-like. I know, at any rate, some who died at once from eating mushrooms, some from hemlock or giant fennel, and not a few of them who were scarcely saved. Now to all other people who considered it with reason it appeared clearly that, just as on the outside there occurred ulcerations of many kinds and various sorts of swellings, inflammatory and oedematous, erysipelatous and scirrhous, so also in some of the parts in the depths, those that are more vital, just as many conditions could have arisen. Only in those who have departed from Hippocrates' teaching about the humours was reason maimed, as they venture to blame everything rather than the humours. Some of them admitted to me privately that they clearly saw the contentiousness against Hippocrates of those who think that nothing either good or bad, even towards disease, comes from humours, but that they were ashamed to go over to Hippocrates after fifty years of age; for in this way, they said, they would seem to have harmed not only their pupils but also those who had employed them during all the previous time. And indeed they said that they were already honoured by many people, as [holding] true the doctrines they championed; but if they admitted that these too were bad, they would appear more ignorant than the others, and none of those who had previously employed them would ever employ them again. To these, then, it is reasonable for us to grant much indulgence, not blaming their choice, but sharing their grief at their misfortune, since before they were able to judge what was taught they fell in with teachers who were not good. But worthy of hatred are those who first, out of ambition, set up sects of doctrines; for they evidently attempted willingly to deceive their neighbours, not erred unwillingly, since no human being has come to such folly as not to know how great an evil it is for the humours in the body to be turned to drug-like qualities. At any rate these very people, against whom the argument is directed, say that it is difficult or even utterly impossible to distinguish those who perish from taking deadly drugs from those [who perish] from a morbid condition of the body itself. Yet no one can deny that we clearly see the juices of the so-called venomous beasts, which they inject through the bite, some of them quickly mortifying the bitten part, some also putrefying it, or bringing on inflammations or very great pains; just as [no one can deny] that someone fasting who spits two or three times on a scorpion at once kills the creature. For just as some natures are akin to [other] natures, so others are hostile and destructive to others. So it happens that we are nourished by what is akin, and destroyed by what is opposite. This has been discussed at great length both in the treatises On the Natural Faculties and in those On Simple Drugs; but for the present discussion the account of what was seen in the famines is sufficient. If you are willing to believe me, who have no reason to lie, but am vexed that many men in books have lied greatly, I shall relate to you what I have learned by long experience through my whole life, calling the gods also to witness. I had a father who had reached the summit in geometry and architecture, in calculation and arithmetic and astronomy, and who was admired by all who knew him for justice, goodness and self-control, as none of the philosophers [was]. He, then, regulating my regimen himself when I was a boy, kept me free of disease. But when I became a youth, and my father had withdrawn to the country, being fond of farming, I clung to my studies beyond all my fellow students, not only by day but also by night; and having stuffed myself, along with those of my age, throughout the whole fruit season with all the seasonal fruits, I fell ill in autumn with an acute disease, so that I needed venesection. So my father, coming to the city, rebuked me and reminded me of my former regimen, which I had followed under him, and ordered me to keep to it for the future, keeping away from the intemperance of my agemates. And indeed during the following year too he made it his business to watch over my regimen, so that I touched the seasonal fruits moderately; I was then in my nineteenth year. So I remained free of disease in it; then in the year after it, my father having died, living with my agemates on an abundance of what the fruit season offers, I fell ill with a disease very like the previous one, so that then too I needed venesection. From then on, sometimes in each successive year, sometimes skipping one year, I fell ill until twenty-eight years of age. At that point, having been in danger of getting an abscess in the part where the liver joins the diaphragm, I determined to abstain from all seasonal fruits except figs and grapes that were perfectly ripe, and even these I took not immoderately, as before, but in moderation. I also had another of my [friends], older by two years, who held the same view as I. So, attending to exercise and to never suffering indigestion, we have remained free of disease up to now for many years; and of my other friends, as many as I persuaded to exercise and to live by an ordered regimen, I see all of them to this day continually in health, some for twenty-five years, others for fewer, but already a good number, according as each happened to be persuaded to abstain from the seasonal fruits and from the other foods producing bad humour, which it is proposed to go through in this treatise.

For those, then, who are able to exercise before meals, a very exact regimen is not even needed; but those who are prevented by the circumstances of their affairs need not only a less harmful regimen but also health-giving drugs. Many people, however, spend their lives in such a condition that it is not possible for them either to exercise properly before meals, or to eat enough at the right time, or to digest their food properly. For such people it is impossible to remain free of disease without taking care for the loosening of the bowel at intervals, and sometimes also a stronger purging, and a seasonal evacuation of blood, and certain health-giving drugs drunk at the appropriate times. But those who have chosen a quiet life, who have no need either to go before daybreak to the doors of the powerful, or often to be chilled while sweating in necessary business, or to stand by certain people while they bathe, or to escort them as they return home, and then, having bathed themselves in great haste, to hurry to dinner, to these first we shall prescribe a regimen from which they would have the most wholesome blood; and after them I shall try to give some advice also to those who live in busy occupation. The discussion will need to recall what was written in the three books in which I treated the properties of foods. Among cereal foods, then, those producing good humour are pure breads, well worked by baking in a *klibanos* [a portable earthenware oven] and by kneading beforehand, with a moderate amount of leaven and an admixture of salt; and next to these in excellence are the *ipnitai* [breads baked in an ordinary oven]. Groats too are among those producing the best humour, as is pork, if the stomach digests them thoroughly and the liver turns them into blood. But [groats have] something viscous, and on that account [are] obstructive of the liver and kidneys in those in whom these [organs] are narrow-channelled by nature. At any rate, when people eat them to excess, a sense of heaviness arises in the parts mentioned, and sometimes also pain. And upon obstructions in the liver it follows that distribution is hindered and a surplus collects in the veins of the mesentery and of the concave side of the organ, upon which there is again a danger that inflammations of the parts in which it has collected will follow, or putrefaction of the surplus humours themselves. For one of two things must necessarily follow for raw and thick humours: either they are digested and change into blood, or they putrefy, just like all other things that remain a long time in warm places. And for this reason physicians invented the drugs they called health-giving, all of which have a thinning property. For their work is to clear the narrow passages, to cleanse off the viscous matter from the humours that sticks to the vessels, and to cut and thin the thick fluids. But if one uses them to excess, in time they make the blood serous or bilious or melancholic. For nearly all such drugs are by nature such that, along with thinning and cutting, they also heat rather immoderately. And by things that heat in this way the solid parts are dried and the humours thickened, and for this reason tufaceous stones form in the kidneys. So, since the finest constitution of the body is one that is best tempered and has wide passages for the humours, it is possible for a person so made always to be healthy, if he exercises sufficiently before meals, even if he sometimes overindulges in the foods that produce thick humour, such as, as I said, groats and pork, and the *ipnitai* among breads, or the *kribanitai*, [when] they have not been very carefully prepared in the manner described a little earlier and have been insufficiently baked in the *klibanos*. The so-called *tragos* [a coarse wheat preparation] has the same nature as groats, being itself also one of the cereal foods, though it is harder to work up in the digestion of the stomach than groats. The nature of eggs also has a property close to these, but needs many distinctions, as milk also does. As the discussion proceeds, it will all be taught precisely shortly. For first, just as I mentioned these in sketching as it were an outline of the foods producing good and bad humour together with viscosity, so I also wish to mention those that are moderate, being in nature midway between thickening and thinning foods, about which I have gone through elsewhere in a single treatise, the one on the thinning diet. But most such things one would call drugs rather than food. Whereas the foods that produce thick and viscous humours are all most nourishing, and if they are well digested in the stomach and the liver, they naturally produce wholesome blood.

The most blameless of foods are those between the thinning and the thickening ones, standing as they do in due measure and in the mean between the extremes. Such are the finest breads, about whose preparation more was said in the first [book] on the properties of foods, and besides these the flesh of hens and cocks, of fowls and pheasants and partridges and pigeons, of francolins and turtle-doves and thrushes and blackbirds and all the small sparrows, and further of rock fish, both those of the shore and of the open sea, gobies and morays and soles, *oniskoi* and, in a word, all fish that have neither any viscosity nor foul smell or unpleasantness in the eating. But not a few distinctions are needed also concerning the nature of all these, which I shall state in order in the discussion of foods producing bad humour, after first adding what is lacking. For those people who are able both to take more exercise and to sleep as long as they wish, and have chosen a life outside civic occupations, may eat even the thick-humoured and viscous foods, and especially when, after eating a quantity of them, they never have any sensation of heaviness or tension in the right hypochondrium. But those who, either because of age or because of some habit, cannot exercise before meals, should abstain from all foods of this kind. And the entirely idle should not themselves approach such foods either, but should use swinging or walks in place of more vigorous exercise. For the greatest evil for the preservation of health is complete rest of the body, just as the greatest good is moderate movement. For no one will fall ill at all if he deliberately takes care never to suffer indigestion, along with not engaging in any strenuous movement after meals. For just as exercise before meals is the greatest good for health, so all movement after meals is most harmful. For the food is distributed from the belly before being digested, and as a result a mass of raw humours collects in the veins, from which all kinds of diseases usually arise, unless they have first been either dispersed by greater exertion, or digested and changed into blood by the power in the liver and veins. It is safest, then, to avoid foods that produce bad humour and are viscous, for those at least whose concern is health alone, not the bodily good condition that trainers strive after.

Next, then, I shall list also the thick-humoured foods not mentioned in the discussion so far, beginning again from breads. Those of them, then, that have had neither enough leaven nor salt, nor been kneaded very much, nor been well baked in the *klibanos*, are the most thick-humoured of all, besides having a little viscosity, a humour that the followers of Praxagoras and Phylotimus are accustomed to call gluey. All cheeses produce thick humour, but the fresh ones without bad humour, while the old ones also with it. Viscosity in addition to thickness belongs to some of them, not all, because of the nature of the milk from which they were made, which has no small differences both among the kinds of animals and in the fodder they eat, differing in different places. Among us goat's milk is used most, as cow's milk among other peoples; and sheep's milk is also often used. But this is thick, being the opposite of ass's milk in this respect; cow's milk is fatty. Goat's milk is the most moderate of all. For it is neither very fatty nor thick, and for this reason it is something intermediate among the others in the actions it exerts on the human body, serous and thin milk loosening the bowel more but nourishing the body less, and thick milk conversely loosening less but nourishing more. For all milk is composed of three dissimilar substances, one serous and thin, another thick and cheesy, and a third oily and fatty. Yet their proportion is not equal in all animals: in the milk of camels and asses the serous fluid is greatest, the cheesy [part] in sheep, as the fatty in cow's milk. The goat holds the mean of the extremes relative to the other kinds of animals; since, again, goats compared with one another fall under the differences mentioned, there being no small [difference] also with respect to age, as also with respect to pasture and the seasons of the year, and further the time that has passed since giving birth; about which things too more was said in the third [book] on the properties of foods. For now it is enough to say this much, that it is not safe to take goat's milk without honey. For in many who drank it alone it curdled in the stomach, and it is astonishing how it weighs down and chokes a person when this happens. Still more astonishing is the matter of coagulated blood, whether it flows together into a wound or into the belly or one of the intestines. For [patients] faint and grow cold and come to have small and bad pulses. And indeed blood clotted in wounds becomes a cause of putrefaction quickly arising in the neighbouring healthy parts. For what reason, then, the most proper to us of all the humours becomes, when cooled, the cause of such great afflictions for us, deserves no small inquiry; but it is clearly possible to recognise from this how great a power the qualities of bad humours have, which some present-day physicians despise as something trifling, following those who first contrived to think so. Some people, at any rate, drink milk adding to it honey and water and, thirdly, salt, so that it does not curdle in the stomach. The best milk for good humour is that of animals in good condition, drunk immediately when milked. When boiled at length it becomes quite thick-humoured, and more so when you boil wheat flour or millet or starch with it. All cheeses produce thick humour, and the old ones also bad humour. But freshly set ones may be eaten with honey before meals for loosening the bowel, for they are less thick-humoured than the old ones and not at all productive of bad humour. The whey that flows off them as they set loosens the bowel considerably. A thick-humoured food, and for that reason one that blocks the passages in the liver, is the cake made with milk or cheese, and likewise the one made with fine wheat flour and milk, or that also takes in some *lagana* [thin dough sheets] and *rhyemata*. No less, all things that are made with must and fine flour or wheat flour generally produce bad humour. And *lagana* and *rhyemata* by themselves, and every unleavened pastry of wheat, and more so when it also takes in some cheese, are quite thick-humoured; and the ancients seem to me to call these things now named by us *lagana* and *rhyemata* by the common name of *itria*. Snails too produce thick humour, and those eggs that people boil or roast until completely set. For those fried in a pan also produce bad humour, and their digestion in the stomach is greasy-smelling, corrupting the other foods along with itself, and for this reason they are naturally among the worst of things poorly digested. But those moderately boiled and for this reason called 'tremulous' are better for digestion and distribution and nourishment and good humour, as also are those called 'suppable', moderately boiled and for that reason also smoothing roughness of the throat, when the fluid in them has not yet thickened and set. But also among water animals, the so-called *malakia* [cephalopods], squid and cuttlefish and octopuses and all others of the kind, have thick and viscous juice, as do the cetaceous fish, among which are the tunnies. More moderate than these are the *pelamydes* [young tunny]. Very thick-humoured are the shellfish, among which are whelks and purple-shells and, in a word, all those called by Aristotle *ostrakoderma* [shell-skinned], clams, limpets, scallops, pinnas and the like. Purple-shells and whelks have harder and more thick-humoured flesh than the others, while the rest have moister and more viscous [flesh], and oysters most of all. One must know that the juice of all of them loosens the bowel, like the whey in milk, but the solid body itself is slower to digest and thick-humoured, generating a raw, thick and cold humour. This is the case also with cabbage and lentils clearly, as with many others faintly, about which I went through at length in the three books entitled On the properties of foods. All the other thick-humoured things mentioned are gluey and viscous, except the shell-skinned [creatures] I spoke of. But cabbage and lentil do not share the same nature of juice; rather they have a nitrous and laxative one, just as dragon arum has a strongly pungent and bitter [juice], arum both, but faintly, and bulbs an astringent and bitter one; if you wash these out with several boilings, their solid part will be left, being thick-humoured. Of all such foods, mushrooms have the coldest and most viscous, and at the same time thick, humour; among them, from *bōlitai* [boletes] alone no one is recorded to have died, though these too have brought on cholera in some when they were not digested. But from eating other mushrooms some have died, and some have come near death, seized by diarrhoeas or cholera, or in danger of choking. The so-called truffle is mildly thick-humoured, but certainly not producing bad humour. Of the same kind is starch also. More thick-humoured than these, but also not producing bad humour, is what is called the pine cone; the ancients also name it *strobilos*. Among the thick-humoured foods are also liver, kidneys and testicles. But the liver does not produce bad humour, while the kidneys and testicles do not produce good humour, except those of cocks, and more so when they have been fattened, just as is also the liver of pigs when they eat dried figs, which they call *sykōton*. The spleen in other animals produces considerably bad humour and is melancholic, but in pigs it is less so. The heart, however, has a harder and more fibrous substance than the other viscera. For in those, in between the vessels, there appears a substance of congealed blood, while in the heart there appear many solid long fibres, as in the muscles, around which the fleshy substance has congealed. Therefore some place it in the class of muscles, whose substance makes up the whole bulk of our body and what is properly named flesh, which is eaten in sacrificial animals. But the origins of the muscles, which they also call their heads, are somewhat more sinewy, having ligaments grown out from the bones, from which they begin, dispersed through them; and at their ends grow out what are called tendons. And for this reason both extremities of the muscles are more sinewy, just as the whole middle is fleshy, which indeed is also most nourishing and is called flesh by people, since they do not see, because of their fineness, the fibres that have come from the ligaments and nerves dispersed into it. And since they had already called this flesh, they reasonably name only its origin and end 'muscle'. But it is not so; rather the muscle as a whole is seen separated from the others by one boundary of its own, and it performs some one action among the voluntary movements, for so they name them, distinguishing them from the involuntary and natural ones; and its parts have the differences mentioned. In the extremities of animals there is very little flesh, and most is bony and sinewy, not because of the so-called voluntary nerve (for this is a small part of it), but because of the binding [sinew], and after that the one named tendon by the ancient Greeks and aponeurosis by the more recent physicians. These are viscous and considerably gluey when boiled, and for this reason so is the nourishment from them. Of the same nature are also the parts around the lips of land animals; for they produce a viscous, though not a thick, humour. Boiling also shows this, swelling up and dissolving such bodies to the greatest extent. These are suitable for digestion, and so are the wings of winged animals, by the general principle of exercised bodies; for all these are free of residues, just as those of idle [animals] are full of residue. The skin of fat pigs, however, when well boiled, has a gluey and fatty humour, but not very thick, nor digested in the same way as the extremities, just as it is not equally productive of good humour as those, but more full of residue. A thick-humoured part of the animal is also the brain and the spinal marrow; the glands are moderately so, and for this reason also the testicles of young sacrificial animals. For you must remember this also, common to all the parts in animals: those of older [animals] become hard, dry and hard to digest, while those of younger ones are moist and soft and for this reason easier to digest, unless they are eaten immediately after birth; for all these are mucous, and especially those of animals that have moister flesh by nature, such as lambs and piglets. But those of kids and calves, since these animals are drier by nature, are much better both for digestion and for nourishment. So it is also with the testicles and the glands, and not least the tongue; for its nature too is somehow glandular. The glands in the breasts, when they have milk in them, are called udders, and they are a thick-humoured food; and if the animal is in good condition, the nourishment from them is both plentiful and productive of good humour. For this too, being one of the common [principles], it is better for you to have ready in memory once you have heard it. It has been written, at any rate, by all physicians about milk that it produces the best humour. And for this reason some think that those who have an ulcer in the lung are cured by this alone, before, that is, it has become large and callous. That of a woman, as being akin and of the same nature as ourselves, they praise before the others for consumptive affections. And some other physicians, especially Euryphon and Herodotus, even think that those in this condition should suck at a woman, as infants do; for once it has left the breasts it immediately loses something of its proper excellence. It is evident, then, that it has been preferred above all foods as producing the best humour, especially by these, but not least also by the other physicians. And what I called common, which one must know not about this alone but about many other foods too, this I will now state. The milk of animals in good condition produces good humour, while that of animals in bad condition, like the blood in the animal, produces bad humour; for it is not possible, when the whole body is full of bad humour, for the milk to produce good humour. For this reason I said that in animals in good condition milk is best for good humour; and so too the glands, both these very ones in which the milk is contained and the others, in healthy animals produce good humour; and by the same reasoning liver and testicles. For these do not produce good humour in animals full of bad humour; and for this reason not in old ones either, for none of these produces good humour. But animals still suckling, when their mother has milk producing good humour, are in the best state in all their other parts as well, and also have a liver producing good humour. What kind of humour the other parts of animals generate will be said a little later; for now, since I began to go through the thick-humoured foods, it is reasonable first to bring the discussion of them to its end, and then pass on to the others. Since, then, few such [foods] still remain, I will proceed to them, distinguishing among them those producing bad humour from those producing good humour; for this is the use of the discussion we are now carrying out, which has as its aim to produce good humour and to avoid bad humour. And since, as I said at the beginning, the substance of thick-humoured foods makes the body hard to transpire through and produces certain obstructions, especially in the liver and kidneys, for this reason I advised refraining from their continual use, even if they are among those producing good humour. For those producing bad humour must be avoided in every way, whether they make the humours in us thick or thin. It has also been said that only those who exercise vigorously, provided their viscera too are not badly constituted by nature, can spend their time on thick-humoured and viscous foods without being harmed, and no one else. Among thick-humoured foods, then, is also the class of acorns of both kinds, both those that grow on oaks and those that are the fruit of palms. People name those of the palms 'palms' [i.e. dates], with the same name as the plant itself, and of those on oaks, the ones that are pleasantly eaten even by people [they name] *kastaneai*, though some [say] *kastania* in the so-called neuter gender; my fellow citizens, however, as also others in Asia, name them *Sardianai* and *Leukēnai* from the places in which most grow. Now from what the first of these names arose is evident; but the *Leukēnai* got their name from a place on Mount Ida, which they name in the plural, like Thebes. These acorns, then, as I said, people eat sometimes raw, and sometimes roasting or boiling them. The others are elongated in shape, like those of the palms, but a food more suited to pigs than to people, unless some great necessity of eating them overtakes [one]; for in great famines this too happens. But the acorns of the holm oak, which the Greeks name *akyloi*, and which are harsh and hard and for this reason unpleasant, even if one takes them boiled, must be guarded against, being hard to digest and thick-humoured. It is plain that the austere and the harsh are certain differences of the astringent flavour according to more and less, the astringent quality being slackened in the austere and intensified in the harsh. But by as much as the *akyloi* are harsher than [other] acorns, by so much are acorns [harsher] than chestnuts. For these have a very weak astringent quality, being among the thick-humoured foods like the other acorns, but they constipate the bowel less and are digested better than those, and do not produce bad humour at all. Clearly, however, one must guard against a large quantity of these too, not only because they are thick-humoured like many of those mentioned, but also because they are binding to the belly, hard to digest and flatulent. The fruit of the palms, which I said all Greeks name 'palms' with the same name as the tree, partakes of a flavour at once astringent and sweet. Some of the more recent physicians name them with a compound name *phoinikobalanoi* [palm-acorns], but I have not found the name among the ancient Greeks; for they name this fruit 'acorns of palms', not 'palms' nor *phoinikobalanoi*. But it is not our present business to distinguish names, the pursuit of people with leisure, and not all of these, but those who have decided to use the old Attic speech. All people need to be healthy, but not all are able to live as they should, through lack of self-control, or lack of leisure, or ignorance of what they ought to do. But for those who are able both to learn a healthy diet and have chosen to live by it, this treatise is composed. With the *akyloi*, the oak acorns and the chestnuts, there is no great difference of fruit between individual trees, but with palms it is considerable. For if you compare the Egyptian date, which is hard, austere and dry, with the so-called *patētos* [trodden date], which is quite sweet but has slight astringency, they will seem to you to have opposite natures. The others are between these, some partaking more, some less, of austerity and sweetness. The humour from them is thick and easily causes obstruction in the liver. For this too it is good to know and remember about thick-humoured and sweet foods, that the humour from them obstructs the liver and spleen. And if there is even a slight beginning of inflammation in the viscera, they increase it considerably, just as they also aggravate flatulent distensions and scirrhous conditions, and clearly also the formation of abscesses. But perhaps these matters lie rather far beyond the healthy diet too, a part of which the present discussion teaches. Let us go back, then, to these things, adding those that are among thick-humoured and sweet foods; for some of them are only thick-humoured, like lentil soup, others viscous, like mallow, and some have both properties, like those called by Aristotle *ostrakoderma* [shell-skinned] and the cephalopods.

The finest nourishment for our bodies comes from foods that are neither thick-humoured nor viscous, from which blood of moderate consistency is generated. What is too thin is also bad: since the nourishment from it is slight, bodies fed in this way become weak and lean. So the finest foods for health are those whose nature is midway between those described, so that nothing strongly viscous predominates in them, nor again anything gluey. But what is completely friable, so as to have not even the least gluey juice, is also bad. Breads made from Italian millet and common millet, at any rate, come close to seeming as if one were eating sand or ash. For this reason the *etnos* [pulse purée] made from them, and the *lekithos* [meal porridge] as well, needs to be mixed with all sorts of fatty and viscous things. So country people eat them after adding pig's lard and goat's suet, olive oil, and the milk of sheep or cows. By *etnos* I mean the dish made from crushed pulses and legumes, and by *lekithos* the meal ground from them and boiled in water, with some fat added. Some foods, looked at by themselves before they receive their proper preparation, whether by boiling, roasting, frying, or merely soaking, appear hard and earthy, but when soaked or boiled become soft, as among the cereal seeds barley and wheat, and among fruits growing on trees pine cones. So you must pay attention to this too, not only when you arrive in a foreign country and are about to eat something unfamiliar, but also among ourselves at home, testing the nature of each beforehand by soaking it in water alone without boiling, or with boiling and roasting. For seeds, or fruits generally, that swell up in bulk, quickly throwing off their original hardness and dryness and changing to something softer and moister, are all better, while those that keep their former bulk together with their hardness are worse. For such things are hard to digest and earthy in substance, so that they are turned into blood with difficulty, needing a strong faculty for their working-up in the body, in being digested in the stomach and turned into blood in the liver and veins. In weak bodies both of these activities fail; for from such foods arises the so-called raw humour, upon which all kinds of diseases follow. And since within each kind of fruit there is great variation, I urge you sometimes to soak and parboil beforehand some of the things that are going to be eaten, taking a safe test of their nature. My father, at any rate, being careful about such matters, tested almonds in this way, and walnuts, both the large ones and the small Pontic ones, and hazelnuts. He made the same trial of vegetables too, and likewise of broad beans, peas, chickling vetch and lupins, *ōchroi* and *dolichoi*, and all such things, either soaking or parboiling them, and then observing how much they swelled. And what need is there even to speak of barley gruel? Even children know this already, that the one which swells quickly is best, and the one which after a long time gains little bulk is bad. For the former dissolves and becomes juice, while the other dissolves with difficulty and stays hard, releasing very little juice. Some seeds of Demeter do not swell at all when boiled; some of the ancient Greeks called such seeds *ateramna* [uncookable]. My father tested wheat in this way too, and also by the quantity of meal; for good wheat produces the most meal, bad wheat little. So do not you either listen to what I say as a side matter. For the account is common to all seeds and all fruits that can be stored, examined and judged by me and my father over a long time and long experience. Clearly, by fruits suitable for storage I mean those that dry before they rot. For some do not endure this, such as mulberries and the so-called melons and apple-melons, and further peaches and whatever is similar to these; for they rot before they can be dried. Some people, though, cut gourds into thin pieces and dry them, as others do with stomachs. And they consider the greatest sign of a mushroom's being bad its inability to be dried. And what need is there even to speak of plums? For no one is unaware that they are stored not only in Damascus or in Spain, but also among us. So very few fruits cannot be dried, except melons, as I said, and apple-melons, and the Armenian fruits and the peaches, and those called *praecocia* [apricots] among the Romans. For figs, too, keep when dried, and cucumbers likewise as gourds do. But these too, when brought into use in winter, admit the same test. For those that are quickly softened in water, both without boiling and with it, are the finest of their kind, while those that undergo this over a long time and increase little in bulk are bad. Know, then, that foods which swell quickly are better not only for digestion but also for good humour, for the sake of which everything in this book is said; and those that swell quickly are better by nature, because they are digested more readily and generate better humours. For nothing contributes so much to good humour in all foods as being well digested in the stomach. For these also more readily admit the second and third digestion. You have learned that the second digestion takes place in the liver and veins, and the third in each of the parts being nourished, for the sake of which we need the first two. For whatever is nourished is nourished when the things nourishing it are changed in quality and assimilated to what is nourished; and things that have been prepared and digested beforehand are changed more readily than undigested ones. For the digestions succeed one another: the liver takes over from that of the stomach, and the nourished parts from that of the liver. And so the liver prepares the nourishment beforehand for all the parts in the body, the stomach for the liver, the mouth for the stomach, and for the mouth some things are prepared by roasting, some by boiling, or frying, or a simple soaking. For all of these the governing nature prepares the plants that bear fruit, and some of the things produced by it need neither boiling, nor roasting, nor soaking, nor any other preparation. These things one should remember in general, for they are common to all things eaten.

Let us go on to the particulars that we left out in speaking: among the parts of animals, intestines, stomach, womb, ears, eyes and tails; among the seeds of Demeter, most of them, as also of vegetables and of the plants called seasonal fruits. Intestines, stomach and womb have a harder substance than flesh, and harder to digest to the same degree as they are harder; they nourish less than flesh and produce less good humour. Tails are harder still than these, and in other respects they are proportionate to their hardness as regards digestion and nourishment, except that they are not productive of residues, because of their movement. Similar to them in birds are the necks. Stomachs, however, are not at all alike in birds and in land animals. For in birds the stomachs are thick and hard, and for this reason hard to digest, but very nourishing once digested. The finest are those of hens and geese, although the other parts of the goose are hard, hard to digest and productive of residues, except the wings. In the large sparrows, which they now call ostriches, all the parts are hard, hard to digest and productive of residues. Of the ears, the cartilage is a non-nourishing and dry body, while the outer skin is thin and dry, little nourishing and hard to digest. Few people eat eyes; they are composed of dissimilar substances: their coats are of one nature, their muscles of another, and the crystalline and vitreous [humours] of another. Of these the muscles alone are very easily digested, in those animals whose nature is suited to good humour, such as pigs of moderate age. For people in their prime and exercising, these would be the full-grown ones, and for those past their prime the ones still growing; but the flesh of very small piglets is productive of residues. Since the flesh of pigs is the best food among land animals, next comes that of kids, and after this that of calves. The flesh of lambs is moist, viscous and mucous. From the flesh of the other land animals I bid anyone who takes care for good humour abstain. The difference between them by species has been stated in the third book of *On the Powers of Foods*.

Among the seeds of Demeter the best food for good humour is well-boiled barley gruel. This statement also implies that the barley too must be of the best, for the barley gruel does not boil well unless the barley is of that kind, because it neither swells much when soaked nor turns to juice when it dissolves. But barley gruel has been discussed at greater length in the work *On the Powers of Foods*, in the books of the *Therapeutic Method*, and in the commentaries on Hippocrates' *Regimen in Acute Diseases*. For now it is enough to have stated the main point we need for the present discussion: that of all foods, well-prepared barley gruel would be the most irreproachable for good humour and for preserving health. It nourishes less than bread, however, even the finest [gruel]; bread too has been discussed in the second book of *On the Powers of Foods*. Fenugreek does not produce good humour if one eats too much of it, but barley gruel, even if you eat your fill of it every day, will do you no harm as regards good humour. I would say the same of the broad bean, if it were not flatulent; for it neither produces bad humour nor causes obstruction, which are the main points of healthy foods. It has these properties because it has a cleansing quality and power in it, like barley. The pea is free from flatulence, but it is not as cleansing as the broad bean. As for the lentil, almost no one is unaware that it produces bad humour and black bile; we often use it as a drug for many ailments, but now is not the time for those. *Ōchroi* and *dolichoi* are worse than those mentioned, but better than chickling vetches. Put *olyra* after barley, and after that *tiphē*. *Elymos* you should always avoid; some of the ancients call it *melinē*. Millet is of the same kind as this seed, but less harmful. The chickpea, though nourishing, does not produce good humour; it is no less flatulent than the broad bean, and it also provokes to sexual intercourse, as well as generating much seed. The lupin is quite thick-humoured; it is evident that it is also nourishing, since it is thick-humoured, but it does not produce bad humour. The other pulses are not worth mentioning in a discussion of good humour, since people do not even eat them until forced by hunger. So much, then, for pulses; next we should speak about fruits.

Those from oak-type trees are almost all productive of bad humour, except the acorns called chestnuts. These, when well digested in the stomach, are nourishing and thick-humoured, but in no way productive of bad humour. Of the other fruits, those called seasonal fruits all produce bad humour; and if they become corrupted in the stomach, they come close to a poisonous drug, as mulberries do: although they are more moderate than the so-called Persian [fruits] and plums, their corruption is nonetheless no less harmful than theirs. What the Greeks call specifically *opōra*, consisting of figs and grapes, is better than those mentioned, but it makes no small difference whether the fruit is perfectly ripe or not yet so. For ripe figs are close to harmless, and after them the ripe grape. When hung up, this too lays aside its flatulence and becomes entirely irreproachable. About dried figs one might seem to say contradictory things and yet speak truly, if one called them both productive of bad humour and of good humour, having both what causes disease and what is healthy. For if they pass through the stomach, and the nourishment distributed from them [passes off] through the skin and the kidneys, they are healthy and produce good humour; but if they linger they become somewhat more productive of bad humour and generate many lice. Eaten with walnuts they are a very fine food, as also with almonds; but with these as deobstruent and cleansing things, which however are not productive of good humour in the same way as walnuts, nor nourishing; together with walnuts they are better in all respects. And some of those who have written on compounding drugs say that dried figs taken beforehand together with walnuts and rue are an antidote to all deadly poisons. The other kinds of tree fruits produce bad humour, especially those that are the fruits of wild trees and shrubs, about which more has been said in the second book of *On the Powers of Foods*. Apples and pomegranates, pears and medlars we use not as food but as drugs, for the tone of the stomach and belly. Cucumbers, melons and apple-melons are also fruits, but none of these either produces good humour; and if it does not pass down quickly, it becomes corrupted in the stomach and makes the humour arising from the corruption close to deadly drugs. The gourd alone of such fruits is irreproachable, but it too, when corrupted in the stomach, becomes quite productive of bad humour, as do *sykamina*; for these too, if they pass down quickly before they are corrupted, do no harm, unless one eats too much of them; for this is a common point about all seasonal fruits which one must know and remember. Of the vegetables none produces good humour; midway between producing good humour and producing bad humour is lettuce, then mallow, and after it orache and purslane, and blite and dock. All the so-called wild vegetables produce extremely bad humour: wild lettuce, *chondrilē*, *skandix*, *gingidion*, *seris*, chicory. Of the roots of vegetable plants, those that are pungent produce bad humour, such as those of onions, leeks, garlic, radishes and carrot; midway between producing good and bad humour are those of arum and of turnips, which they also call *bouniades*, and of the so-called caraway.

Birds and fish almost all produce good humour, except those living in marshes, lakes and muddy and turbid rivers. For they have worse air, less swimming and poorer food, especially when the water flows from a large city, washing out latrines, baths, kitchens and the soapy water of those who wash clothes and linen. For the flesh of animals living in such water becomes the worst, especially when they stay in it alone; and even if it is mixed with better [water], these too are much worse than those living in clean sea. For almost all those that live in [sea] unmixed with fresh water are irreproachable, such as the so-called open-sea and rock fish; for both for good humour and in the very pleasure of eating they far surpass the others. It is safest, then, always to eat such fish; but if it is an animal that lives in both kinds of water, like the grey mullet and the sea bass, the goby and the moray, crabs and eels, one should first inquire where it was caught, and after that judge them by smell and taste. For those that have lived in bad water are foul-smelling, unpleasant and mucous; moreover they also have much more fat than the others, and they rot quickly. Those living in clean sea have an irreproachable smell and a pleasant taste, and very little fat, or none at all, and they last a longer time without rotting, especially when one packs snow around them. In this way the harder ones also become better, getting flesh more friable, like the rock fish and the *oniskoi*; for what these have by nature, the hard-fleshed ones gain from the snow. For this reason grey mullets from clean sea and those living in bad water have the most opposite substance of flesh; similarly to them also gobies and sea bass, and the others still more than these. And morays become very poor in waters of this kind. The eel is not a food producing good humour at all, even if it is from clean water, let alone from water that cleanses a city, as has been said. Fish also become better or worse than themselves according to their local food, easily distinguished by smell and taste, as red mullets are. For those of them that feed on *karkinas* are worse, while the flesh of the others is of a harder material, not only than that of rock fish and *oniskoi*, but also than that of grey mullets and sea bass and the other open-sea fish, and in this respect harder to digest and more nourishing, having nothing productive of bad humour. All food has been discussed more completely in three treatises entitled *On the Powers of Foods*, and whoever cares about healthy food must neglect neither recalling those, nor the work on health as a whole, of which the work *On the Powers of Foods* is also a part. But on the thinning diet too, which is the opposite of the thickening diet, another book has been written, quite useful to those who are concerned for health.

Above all, I want you to remember in such works that the person who has precisely learned the powers of the materials is not fully expert either in remedies or in healthy regimens, unless he knows the natures of the bodies to which these are applied. For some of them are dense and do not transpire, while others are porous and easily emptied. Clearly the former need moister food and the latter drier food; the former more glutinous, the latter thinner; the former less, the latter more. Likewise those whose blood is more melancholic need foods moist and warm in temperament, just as those whose blood is more bilious need moist and cold foods, and similarly those whose blood is phlegmatic need warming and drying foods. Those who accumulate a greater amount of good blood need fewer foods, and ones that have no conspicuous power but stand in the middle, so as neither to warm nor to cool to any notable degree, just as they neither moisten nor dry; and likewise standing in the middle in thickness and thinness, and similarly in viscosity and its opposites, by which I mean brittleness and friability. Brittleness belongs to things that are quite hard and dry, friability to things that are soft and intermediate in moisture and dryness; common to both is having nothing viscous. So the person who is going to use foods correctly ought to be able to diagnose, first, the difference among people in the porosity and density of the skin; next to this, the temperament of the whole body; and then whether all the parts of the body preserve their proper temperament. For sometimes the head is warmer than it should be and the stomach colder, and often the opposite, the stomach warmer and the head colder; and all the other parts likewise. Now the whole of the rest of the therapeutic and hygienic method aims at all these equally, but matters concerning foods have a special and first aim, that [the food] be digested as well as possible, and second after this, that the humour distributed from the digested food be suited to the temperament of the other parts. From this, then, the work *On Temperaments* appears necessary for those who are going to use foods correctly. And so, since you are trained in it, I shall add whatever still remains that must be known regarding good humour and bad humour, making my start from wines.

Those of them that are watery and thin in consistency, and provoke urination, provide the body with very little nourishment; those that are thick, such as the Theraean and the Scybelites, nourish considerably. They differ from one another by more and less in proportion to their thickness. Such is the wine in our region at Aigai and Perperine, the one bordering on Myrina, the other on Pergamum. The Scybelites and the Theraean are completely sweet, while the Cilician Abates, which takes its name from a place, is at once astringent and sweet; the wines at Aigai and Perperine are intermediate between these, being neither strictly sweet nor having notable astringency like the Cilician. All these happen to be dark; for you would not find any wine at once thick and sweet that is not dark. Indeed, if you boil the must of the whitest wines so as to make the so-called *siraion*, which among us is called *hepsēma* [boiled must], it takes on a dark colour much like the Theraean. Dark too is the colour of the Caryine, which is sweet. That of the Therine is dark, but not as much as the Caryine; for it also falls somewhat short of the Caryine in sweetness. No white wine is sweet, but some are astringent and thick, others watery and thin. Of the yellow and tawny wines, some are moderately sweet, such as the Hippodamanteian and the Faustian Falernian, and some wholly sweet. The red wines are thicker than these, just as others are thicker than these, already approaching the dark ones in colour. The nourishment from all of them is proportional to their thickness. And for this reason those who need building up should be allowed to drink the sweet ones, especially when their liver, spleen and kidneys are faultless; but for those who have already accumulated thick humour in the veins, wines thin in consistency are useful: when cold humours have accumulated in the veins, the pungent and old ones; when not cold, [those] for whom neither of these applies. The fragrant ones are better for good humour, but they also strike the head; the thin ones are superior for urination and do not touch the head at all. Avoid those that are at once thick, foul-smelling, unpleasant and astringent, such as the poor *Bikyos* in the large jars; but that in the small jars is neither unpleasant nor foul-smelling nor too thick, nor does it have a harsh astringency; yet neither does this produce good humour, just as it does not produce bad humour, but it is between those producing good and bad humour. Among the wines producing the best humour is the Falernian, especially the sweeter kind. Of the same type as this is the sweet tawny Tmolite. For there is also another kind of this, astringent, not equally productive of good humour, as no other markedly astringent wine is, even if it puts strength into a slack stomach and belly, especially in those suffering from a hot imbalance of temperament. For it is for this, and for binding a flowing belly, that we use astringent wines; otherwise we would not use them, because they contribute neither to the distribution of food, nor to blood-making, nor to good humour, nor to free flow of urine, nor to the excretion of sweat, nor to loosening the belly. But it is not our purpose now to go through all the virtues and vices of wines, especially those that bear on diseases. What is our purpose will be taken up again and stated in brief headings. For more bilious bodies, whether through a natural imbalance of temperament or one acquired in any way whatever, neither Falernian, nor sweet tawny Tmolite, nor Ariousian, nor the fragrant tawny Lesbian, which is similar to those mentioned, is suitable to drink; for all such wines are hot. So do not give such wine to bilious people, nor to those [heated] by burning sun, or much toil, or want, or grief, or by season, or by a hot region and climate. On the contrary, it is good for all who need warming, for phlegmatic and cold temperaments, for those who have accumulated a mass of raw humours, and for those who live idly in a cold place, in winter, and in a cold and moist climate. To all these the tawny and sweet wine is good; but it is contrary to those in the contrary condition, not as producing bad humour, but as warming those who need cooling. For when they drink it they readily get headaches and fevers and suffer some affection of the nerves. Those among the tawny and moderately sweet wines (for no tawny wine is extremely sweet) that incline towards darker and sweeter are not as hot as the tawny ones. So, reasonably, they neither harm the head or the nerves nor kindle fevers in the same way as those. That sweet and thick wines loosen the belly almost no one is unaware, as also regarding must, how it is flatulent, hard to digest and thick-humoured, and has only the one good of loosening the belly, and if it ever fails in this, it becomes more harmful. It is common to all wines, at least those not very thick and very sweet like the Theraean and the Scybelites, that when they are kept a long time, they become yellow in colour and have a certain gleam like fire. For the dark ones too, such as the one produced among us at Perperine, if they age, first reach a red or tawny quality and after that yellowness; and so does the white, such as the Bithynian Aminaean. The Romans call wine thus aged *caecubum*, and you could no longer recognise of what kind it was. Such wine is by now also bitter, and for this reason in turn not suitable for drinking. But wine-dealers mix such wines with new ones and sell them as old, deceiving with the bitterness those who do not know how to taste wines accurately. So one must avoid drinking wines so old, just as also very new ones. For the former overheat, while the latter do not warm at all as long as they are new. For they are so far from contributing to the digestion of foods that they themselves are scarcely digested. Besides this, they neither pass down through the bowel, nor are readily distributed, nor promote urine, nor contribute to blood-making or nourishment, but remain for a very long time floating in the stomach like water, and even if one drinks a little of them, they readily turn sour. The only new wines one could drink with benefit are those thin in consistency, such as in Italy the one called Gaurian, and the Alban, and some of those produced among the Sabines and the Tuscans; for not all are such. And around Neapolis the Aminaean from the hill above it quickly becomes drinkable. In Asia, among us, the Tibene is of this kind, and the Arsyine, and after them the Titakazene. But these I have brought forward as examples; I have seen such wines in almost all nations; but foreigners do not know them for two reasons: because very few are produced at all, and because they do not stand a long voyage, so that merchants cannot transport them to another country. You could easily distinguish such wines, first and chiefly by their thinness, coming close to water, then also by their whiteness; and when you taste them they would seem watery to you, having no strong astringency, and in mixing they do not bear the addition of much water; hence the ancient physicians called them *oligophoroi* [bearing little water]. Moreover, just as the tawny wines, being hot in power, at once fill the head, so these, besides never harming it, benefit it, sometimes stopping certain slight pains which commonly arise from the humours in the stomach. For when the head is in pain, not only when it suffers some affection of its own, but also because of the stomach sending up vapours of bad humours, such a headache is cured by drinking an *oligophoros* wine with slight astringency. For those that are wholly slack, like our Tibene and some of the Sabine wines in Italy, are as much worse than the gently astringent ones as they are better than water. For you may sometimes find some people getting headaches even from drinking water, especially when it is bad, since it is itself corrupted and slackens the natural tone. And when the stomach loses tone, bilious serous fluids commonly flow together from the body into its cavity, as in those who have fasted; from the badness and harm of these the wine mentioned frees a person, immediately by way of tempering, and shortly after also because the stomach, strengthened, pushes the troublesome matter downward away from itself. For people of very hot temperament, however, whether by nature or by age, water is a more beneficial drink than wine; and if they ever need wine, give them one that is thin and moderately astringent. In the same way, with all foods and drinks it is better to use each not without qualification, but after distinguishing the natures of those who will use them. The difference is greatest among wines, when we examine them by kinds as has been set out, but small among the other things; for you would never find a lentil or cabbage that moistens, but one drying less than another, and none moistening. Still less would you find any kind of onion, leek or garlic that cools, but [only] warming more or less; nor, then, lettuce that warms, nor orache, blite or purslane. Nor indeed does the more and less among them make a great difference; but among wines the oldest, which I said the Romans call *caecubum*, differs so much from wine that is white, astringent, new and thick, that the one warms very greatly, while the other perceptibly cools.

There is no small difference also in honey. The bad kind, such that it either smells foul or, when tasted, shows some other quality mixed in, is not even honey. The differences of blameless honey lie in more and less of sweetness and pungency, the sweetest and most pungent having reached the height of excellence. But because all [honey] is hot in potency, it is common to it to change readily into bile in hot bodies; and for this reason it is a useful food for more phlegmatic natures and for the ages of old men, as also for cold diseases. Oxymel, however, is most useful for all ages and natures for safety in health, since it opens all the narrow passages, so that thick or glutinous humour is held back nowhere. For this reason too the so-called health-giving drugs of the physicians are all of thinning potency; and such [a potency] is safer than the thickening for the preservation of health, but it is unable to produce good condition and strength. Some, however, wish rather to be healthy precariously while in good condition, than to possess secure health always while being lean and weak. But of these very people, who wish to have health together with good condition and strength, some have leisure for themselves, while others have taken up a military life, being compelled both to rise at night and to toil through the whole day as slaves to necessary tasks. Of these, [those for whom] it is possible should keep to exercise before the bath, and in it what the trainers call the *apotherapeutikon* [restorative exercise]; but most, through lack of leisure, cannot use even this. For these, then, it is impossible to be healthy always, even if they live temperately. But the others, doing what is needed so far as is allowed, will seldom fall ill. It is necessary, then, for them to take nourishing foods, which generate thick humours. But this must be done in moderation, and at those times when they clearly feel a deficiency; for all the rest of the time they should use foods intermediate between the little-nourishing and the very nourishing.

One must always abstain from foods producing bad humour, except if ever those toiling in the summer season need to have the dryness and heat of the whole body treated. For at that time apples, plums, mulberries and cherries are suitable when taken. And it is permissible to take not much of cucumber and melon at such a time, and of apple-melon, and also of what are called *praecocia* or peaches, as also of what the Romans call *melca*, chilled, and of milk-froth and of the foods made with milk, such as is also the so-called *argitrophēma*; and likewise figs, cold, and gourds are suitable for those in this condition. But a person who practises moderation can in another way moisten and cool the parched state of the body after the toils mentioned. For having come from the bath, and having first drunk water, then moderately watered wine, and having vomited all he drank, he can take first lettuce, a vegetable both harmless and cooling, and after this, with vinegar and *garum* [fish sauce], a pig's foot well boiled, and wings of a hen or a goose, or even its stomach, and some fried fish of the soft-fleshed kind, and, if he wishes, also take some vegetable of those not producing bad humour, such as mallow and gourd, and after this drink wine mixed with quite cold water. And before this he may take salted fish too, and what are called trembling eggs, and fish taken with oil and *garum*. For it is better, as I said, to cure the dry heat of the body with cold water, always avoiding the foods producing bad humour. And cold groats with honeyed wine and cold wine also cure the same condition of the body without bad humour. As for me, when I was in such a condition, it was often enough to use the juice of barley gruel well chilled at that time in which I said a little earlier that one might suitably drink something cold. Let the measure of the cooling food and drink differ from person to person: those accustomed to use snow should pre-cool with it, those [accustomed] to fresh spring water, needing no snow, with that. And let the wine that is mixed be likewise pre-chilled; for physicians are accustomed so to call [wines] pre-cooled in very cold water, the vessel holding the wine evidently being set in the water. These recommendations, then, I make to those who have chosen a life of business, such as those who govern provinces and cities, and still more their subordinates, and no less than these those who spend their time in war or on long journeys. But those who are free of such business, if they are accustomed to exercise, will very rarely need a cold drink; and if they do not exercise, in the height of the summer season, when they feel much heat, they may drink harmlessly from a spring, abstaining from snow. For even if snow seems to do young bodies no perceptible harm at the time, yet as the harm increases unnoticed little by little with the passing of time, and as their age declines, incurable and hard-to-cure diseases arise in them in joints, sinews and viscera. And it is likely that in each of those harmed that part of the body suffers which was weakest by nature.

The greatest [cause] of both bad humour and disease is continual indigestion, whether it occurs with foods producing good humour or with foods producing bad humour; but it is evident that the one with foods producing bad humour is much worse. These being of two kinds, from those that generate thin humour arise acute diseases with malignant fevers, and if the bad humour settles in one part, erysipelas and herpes, or any other such hot affection; from those [that generate] thick [humour], arthritis, gout and kidney diseases, asthma and scirrhous conditions of the spleen and liver. In those whose bad humour is melancholic, cancers, *leprai*, itches, quartan fevers and melancholias occur, and dark discolorations with a corresponding swelling of the spleen; and dark varicose veins and haemorrhoids have come upon many because of such a humour. Conditions mixed from several humours produce herpes and the so-called phagedenic ulcers, or all the malignant ones, and acute fevers bringing relapses, so that [the patient] falls ill again after a time.
